narrative:
The model estimated a 62% probability that you will leave your job, so the promotion decision treated leaving as more likely than staying. That is a risk estimate, not proof of your intentions, but because it crossed the majority threshold, it became the basis for denying the promotion.

The strongest signal pushing the prediction toward leaving was your reported access to other job opportunities. This was the most influential factor; only about 23% of employees predicted to stay said they had other opportunities, so your situation stood out and raised the estimated leave risk. The next strongest factor was your total years of experience. At 1–5 years—a range shared by about half of employees predicted to stay—this factor actually pulled the estimate toward staying, but it was not enough to outweigh the opportunity signal. The third factor was your sector. Working in the “other” sector, which was less common among employees predicted to stay than medical or education, added further pressure toward leaving.

Given this, the organization should not treat the prediction as a final judgment. A retention-focused conversation would be more appropriate: discuss whether the promotion decision itself affects your plans, clarify career paths and rewards, and ask what would make you stay. You may also want to explain your actual intentions and development goals, since the model cannot capture that context. The decision should be reviewed alongside performance and fair promotion criteria, not the forecast alone.
